source.version_note: International Journal of Social Robotics 13(4), 691–701, July 2021 issue; first online 18 June 2020. The file’s 2021 year and 2020 DOI/online date refer to legitimate different publication stages.
source.verification_method: All eleven supplied pages, the single model figure, six tables, footnotes, declarations,39 references and author biographies read. Publisher/Crossref verify main identity/dates. Four targeted cited-record checks distinguish a conference paper from a journal article and repair names/locators. No supplement/data section found in the inspected publisher page; no original data, stimuli archive, code or preregistration obtained.

citation.title: I, Robot: How Human Appearance and Mind Attribution Relate to the Perceived Danger of Robots

reading.source_scope_note: Three online, within-person student photo-rating studies compare selected mechanical, humanoid and android robots. The study measures appearance, category-boundary questions, attributed capacities and perceived potential identity/social damage, not actual robot danger, human dehumanization or observed real-world harm.
access_limits: The single conceptual diagram and all six tables visually inspected, including99% interval endpoints that qualify claims of full mediation. The third study uses different pictures, not identical stimulus replication.

No supplementary-information or data-availability section was found in the inspected publisher page. This does not establish that no additional materials exist. The paper asks readers to contact the author for example stimuli; no contact was initiated.

Full original pictures, questionnaire item sets, participant-level records, exclusions, registration, MEMORE syntax and bootstrap output were not obtained. Scale examples and all reported reliabilities were read, but no reanalysis or code execution performed.

Cited original distinctiveness, intergroup, mind-perception and uncanny-valley studies/books were not independently fully read. Targeted Crossref checks verify bibliography identities/locators only and receive no separate full-paper credit.

study.sample: Study 1 n55,44 female/11 male, mean age19.5; Study 2 n60,52 female/5 male/3 unknown, mean19.3; Study 3 n67,57 female/8 male/2 unknown, mean19.1. Total182 study participations, not independently verified unique people. Convenience samples are young Radboud students receiving course credit, not representative adults or robot users.
study.design: Each participant rates twelve pictures, four robots per category, in random photo order. Mechanical/humanoid/android category varies within person. Studies 1–2 use earlier Ferrari stimuli; Study 3 uses new full-body images with more controlled backgrounds, and mechanical robots there also have arms/head. Category comparison bundles shape, robot identity and other image features.
study.measures: Appearance has three items, for example mistaking the robot for a real person. The three-item distinctiveness measure includes asking what differences exist between robots and humans; higher table values denote more boundary blurring/threat, not greater distinctiveness. Four damage items concern perceived possible harm to people/relationships/identity. All use1–7 ratings, not measured actual safety incidents.
study.mind: Studies 2–3 add18 capacity adjectives,7 agency and11 experience, summarized by robot category. High alpha does not establish genuine machine mind or universal factor architecture. Appearance, category ambiguity and a felt motivation to be unique are related but different constructs.
study.analysis: The paper explicitly uses within-participant MEMORE difference-score mediation,1000 bootstrap samples and99% confidence intervals for the three pairwise category comparisons. This is not an analysis treating all robot ratings as independent people.99% intervals are more conservative than the usual98.33% Bonferroni interval for three .05-family contrasts; no correction failure is inferred merely because99 rather than98.33 is used.
study.mediation_limits: Measured within-person mediators remain nonrandomized. The figure suggests a chain, but reported analyses separately test distinctiveness→damage and appearance/mind→distinctiveness, rather than one jointly identified serial/competing-mediator causal model. A nonsignificant direct effect does not establish a complete causal mechanism.
study.study_1: All three category comparisons have positive total/indirect effects through distinctiveness on damage and through appearance on distinctiveness. Table2’s n55 descriptive values belong to Study 1 despite its erroneous Study 2 caption. Android appearance/distinctiveness/damage means are5.57/5.76/4.12 versus mechanical1.67/1.89/2.02.
study.study_2_appearance: Appearance indirect effects are positive in all three comparisons, but mechanical versus humanoid retains a positive direct effect .547,99%CI[.14,.96]. The text’s full-mediation claim for every comparison is too broad.
study.study_2_mind: Experience indirect effects all include zero. Agency has one positive indirect effect for humanoid versus android,.469,99%CI[.03,.85], alongside a direct effect. The body acknowledges that exception. An absence of a stable pattern is not an absence of every indirect effect.
study.study_3_distinctiveness: All three distinctiveness→damage indirect effects exclude zero, but mechanical versus humanoid direct effect .160,99%CI[.01,.31] also excludes zero. The repeated full-mediation statement should be qualified for that contrast.
study.study_3_appearance: Appearance mediation fails for mechanical versus humanoid,.188,99%CI[−.05,.45], despite a positive total .434. The other two appearance indirect effects are positive. Thus even the appearance path is not uniformly significant across all comparisons and stimulus sets.
study.study_3_mind: Experience has one positive indirect effect, mechanical versus android,.891,99%CI[.13,1.55]. Agency has positive indirect effects for mechanical versus android,.537,[.14,.96], and humanoid versus android,.624,[.16,1.13]. These real exceptions must be preserved despite the abstract’s broad negative summary.
study.correlations: Exploratory agency/experience–damage correlations vary by category and study. Mechanical-agency correlation .369,p.004 in Study 2 becomes .128,p.301 in Study 3, while android correlations become significant in Study 3. No formal comparison of dependent correlations is supplied; unequal significance does not establish that correlations differ.
study.nonmonotonic_capacity: In Study 3 mechanical robots have agency3.44 versus humanoid2.99 and experience2.10 versus2.07, while androids are higher. Physical humanlikeness and attributed mind are not one interchangeable monotonic dimension.
study.generality: The authors explicitly discuss still images, weak/unstable mind paths, possible limited power and the young convenience sample. Calls to retain robotic features, increase acceptance or use shared goals are design proposals and cited discussion, not tested interventions or validated real-world risk prevention.

summary: No new row: strengthen Human-distinctiveness threat, Anthropomorphism, Agency attribution and Experience attribution with direct photo-rating evidence and mixed paths. Correct overbroad mediation summaries and bibliography identity errors while preserving the actual repeated-measure analysis and conservative intervals.

findings.definition: A perceived challenge to attributes regarded as uniquely human that threatens a person's sense of human identity or distinctiveness.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: A three-item boundary-blurring measure and four-item perceived-damage measure vary across selected robot categories in three within-person samples. Appearance-related indirect paths are generally more consistent than capacity-related ones. This adds direct operational evidence to entries previously supported by secondary discussion.
findings.boundary: Boundary questions, a felt threat to identity, actual loss of human worth and real robot danger differ. Measured mediation does not identify one cause. Human dignity/rights are not reduced by machine capability, and the study does not measure AI subjective threat.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Ratings of selected robot photos show appearance→boundary-blurring indirect effects in most pairwise comparisons; Study 3 mechanical/humanoid is an exception. Pictures differ on many features and actual interaction is not tested.
findings.boundary: A humanlike image, attributed mind and genuine mental capacity are distinct. Proposed acceptance-oriented design recommendations do not prove a universal optimal humanlike level or actual safety benefit.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 humanoid/android and Study 3 mechanical/android plus humanoid/android have positive agency indirect effects on boundary blurring, with 99% intervals excluding zero. Other comparisons are null, and correlations with perceived damage vary.
findings.boundary: The abstract’s broad absence wording must retain these exceptions. No direct comparison establishes agency effects equal to, weaker than or different from appearance effects. Attributed planning is not actual autonomy, moral responsibility or sentience.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Experience indirect effects are null in Study 2 but positive for mechanical/android in Study 3,.891,99%CI[.13,1.55]. Other Study 3 contrasts include zero. The paper acknowledges unstable results and changed stimulus sets.
findings.boundary: A null comparison is not equivalence, a significant exception is not a universal mechanism and changed pictures do not isolate experience. Ratings of emotional capacity do not establish actual robot feelings.

findings.definition: Perceiving possible harm to the value, meaning or expression of an identity one holds.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The discussion connects boundary blurring with perceived human identity/social damage and proposes alternative roles for closeness or familiarity. The measure is specific to robots and human-category perceptions.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only clarification: generic identity threat, human uniqueness concerns, actual status loss and objective danger are not interchangeable. No independently manipulated generic identity-threat process is demonstrated.

findings.definition: A drop in comfort or affinity when an artificial agent appears highly, but imperfectly, human-like, rather than a steady increase as human likeness rises.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named attribution/threat constructs already exist. Add the source’s actual scale, repeated-measure design, mixed indirect effects and limits instead of adding a synonymous mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The introduction invokes the uncanny valley and prediction mismatch, but the actual dependent measure concerns perceived potential human/identity damage. Only three selected appearance categories and still pictures are tested.
findings.boundary: The study does not directly measure a nonlinear eeriness valley, motion mismatch, neural prediction error or objective danger. Keep this as contextual boundary evidence rather than an extra empirical uncanny-valley demonstration.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The lower endpoint is printed[−01,.50], missing a clear decimal separator. It could mean−.01, but no original output was obtained; do not invent the endpoint.

The printed Wiley SICI DOI loses delimiters and appears malformed. The source identity is not independently fully resolved here; a failed or malformed locator is not proof that the paper is fabricated.

Only scale examples and category summaries are supplied. No full image set, all-item scoring, exclusions, original syntax, stimulus random-effect treatment or saved bootstrap distribution was inspected.

The stated99% intervals conservatively address three pairwise comparisons, but the family definition across all mediator models and exploratory correlations is not fully specified. No formal dependent-correlation comparison or joint appearance-versus-mind indirect-effect comparison is supplied.

methodological_limits: Young, mostly female convenience samples rating still pictures do not represent all ages/cultures or real robot interaction. Repeated ratings and twelve images are not independent people or a random sample of all robot designs.

Within-person MEMORE analysis explicitly addresses repeated category ratings. It should not be criticized as treating every response independently, while its measured mediators and fixed selected stimuli still limit causal generalization.

High distinctiveness-score values indicate more boundary questioning/blurring in this instrument, not greater preserved distinctiveness. Perceived possible identity/social damage is not objective danger, actual harm, dehumanization of humans or measured neural prediction error.

Appearance and mind paths are tested separately; one significant and another nonsignificant path is not a formal difference. Positive exceptions and the null Study 3 mechanical/humanoid appearance path must remain visible.

No significant direct effect does not prove full mediation. Two reported direct intervals exclude zero despite full-mediation prose; a jointly identified causal chain is not estimated by the separate models shown.

The 99% intervals are conservative for three pairwise tests. With 1000 bootstrap samples, extreme-tail endpoints can be imprecise; that is a precision limit rather than proof all intervals are invalid.

Separate category correlations vary across studies; unequal significance is not a correlation-difference test. Image changes are acknowledged, so inconsistency cannot uniquely identify a psychological moderator.
Attributed capacities, identity threat, aesthetic appearance, closeness and acceptance differ. The study does not demonstrate genuine machine experience or a universally safe/acceptable design.

Authors’ own discussion acknowledges static stimuli, small/limited samples and unstable mind paths. No claims of globally absent mediation, real eldercare benefit or actual identity damage are carried into the ontology.
No author contact, raw data, code execution, complete cited-book reading, original-source effect replication or new term/source quota is claimed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: That source invokes human-distinctiveness threat as an unmeasured explanation. This photo study adds direct instrument-level evidence, but the instrument and threat/damage interpretations still need their own limits.
Broader identity threat and human–machine distinctiveness are related but distinct. Direct operational evidence here does not retroactively make a secondary discussion an independent replication.
Appearance, agency, experience and eeriness should not be collapsed into one scale or mechanism. Repeated-measure methods and actual null/positive exceptions must be described specifically.

This study concerns perceived identity damage after robot photos, whereas the prior paper measures later human-quality ratings and choices. Do not equate boundary blurring with actual human dehumanization or infer the same pathway solely from shared vocabulary.

deferred.term: Need for distinctiveness as another newly measured behavior
deferred.reason: It is a motivational background account, whereas the actual instrument asks about category boundaries and perceived damage. Do not relabel a cause, threatened state and observed scale as independent mechanisms without a separate primary definition/measurement review.

deferred.term: Uncanny valley of mind as another established result
deferred.reason: The term is cited background. This paper does not directly measure eeriness, a nonlinear valley or the original autonomous-avatar manipulation.
Perceived-risk ratings and separate measured mediations under fixed stimuli do not identify actual damage or a universal causal pathway.

limitations: No new entry; direct evidence enriches existing constructs. Eleven categories, stable IDs and unnumbered rows retained. No invented annual data, forced citation quota, automatic ethical/harm edges, author messages or full-paper Markdown transcription.
